text: You already know how to write a Kubernetes Deployment or Service as YAML. Putting those files in a Git repo feels like an obvious next step, and plenty of teams stop right there. GitOps asks for something stricter: Git isn't just a copy of your config, it's declared to be the copy that matters. If the live cluster ever disagrees with what's committed on the default branch, the cluster is wrong and Git is right, full stop.

That distinction rests on imperative versus declarative. Kubectl scale deployment payments-api --replicas=5 tells the cluster what to do right now, with no durable record of why. A manifest with replicas: 5 tells the cluster what the end state should look like, and the control plane figures out how to get there. Run kubectl apply on that file once or a thousand times and you get the same result. That idempotent, diffable quality is exactly what makes declarative config trackable in Git in the first place.

This is OpenGitOps's first principle, straight from the CNCF working group: a system managed by GitOps must have its desired state expressed declaratively. Not scripts that run commands, actual descriptions of the end state, like the deployment you're looking at here. It's why the manifests you already write are a prerequisite for GitOps, not incidental to it.

The second principle is versioned and immutable: desired state must be stored with full version history and immutable snapshots. Git satisfies that almost by accident. Every commit is immutable and content-addressed, git log shows a complete history of every change, and git revert undoes a bad one by creating a new commit rather than guessing at a previous state. A repo laid out with a shared base and per-environment overlays, like staging and production here, makes every change go through a pull request, so the cluster never sees anything that didn't pass through that door.

So far this is really just good repo hygiene — nothing is actually enforcing that the cluster matches Git yet. Next lesson covers the other half of that story: how changes actually get from this repo onto a live cluster, and why GitOps insists an in-cluster agent pulls them, instead of a CI pipeline pushing them in.
